      <content name="title">Guide to Good Posture</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Posture</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Good posture is about more than standing up straight so you can look your best. It is an important part of your long-term health. Making sure that you hold your body the right way, whether you are moving or still, can prevent pain, injuries, and other health problems.</p>What is posture?<p>Posture is how you hold your body. There are two types:</p><ul><li>Dynamic posture is how you hold yourself when you are moving, like when you are walking, running, or bending over to pick up something.</li><li>Static posture is how you hold yourself when you are not moving, like when you are sitting, standing, or sleeping.</li></ul><p>It is important to make sure that you have good dynamic and static posture.</p><p>The key to good posture is the position of your spine. Your spine has three natural curves - at your neck, mid back, and low back. Correct posture should maintain these curves, but not increase them. Your head should be above your shoulders, and the top of your shoulder should be over the hips.</p>How can posture affect my health?<p>Poor posture can be bad for your health. Slouching or slumping over can:</p><ul><li>Misalign your <span class="qt0">musculoskeletal</span> <span class="qt1">system</span></li><li>Wear away at your spine, making it more fragile and prone to injury</li><li>Cause neck, shoulder, and back pain</li><li>Decrease your flexibility</li><li>Affect how well your joints move</li><li>Affect your balance and increase your risk of falling</li><li>Make it harder to digest your food</li><li>Make it harder to breathe</li></ul>How can I improve my posture in general?<p>
</p><ul><li>Be mindful of your posture during everyday activities, like watching television, washing dishes, or walking</li><li>Stay active. Any kind of exercise may help improve your posture, but certain types of exercises can be especially helpful. They include yoga, tai chi, and other classes that focus on body awareness. It is also a good idea to do exercises that strengthen your core (muscles around your back, abdomen, and pelvis).</li><li>Maintain a healthy weight. Extra weight can weaken your abdominal muscles, cause problems for your pelvis and spine, and contribute to low back pain. All of these can hurt your posture.</li><li>Wear comfortable, low-heeled shoes. High heels, for example, can throw off your balance and force you to walk differently. This puts more stress on your muscles and harms your posture.</li><li>Make sure work surfaces are at a comfortable height for you, whether you're sitting in front of a computer, making dinner, or eating a meal.</li></ul>How can I improve my posture when sitting?<p>Many Americans spend a lot of their time sitting - either at work, at school, or at home. It is important to sit properly, and to take frequent breaks:</p><ul><li>Switch sitting positions often</li><li>Take brief walks around your office or home</li><li>Gently stretch your muscles every so often to help relieve muscle tension</li><li>Don't cross your legs; keep your feet on the floor, with your ankles in front of your knees</li><li>Make sure that your feet touch the floor, or if that's not possible, use a footrest</li><li>Relax your shoulders; they should not be rounded or pulled backwards</li><li>Keep your elbows in close to your body. They should be bent between 90 and 120 degrees.</li><li>Make sure that your back is fully supported. Use a back pillow or other back support if your chair does not have a backrest that can support your lower back's curve.</li><li>Make sure that your thighs and hips are supported. You should have a well-padded seat, and your thighs and hips should be parallel to the floor.</li></ul>How can I improve my posture when standing?<p>
</p><ul><li>Stand up straight and tall</li><li>Keep your shoulders back</li><li>Pull your stomach in</li><li>Put your weight mostly on the balls of your feet</li><li>Keep your head level</li><li>Let your arms hang down naturally at your sides</li><li>Keep your feet about shoulder-width apart</li></ul><p>With practice, you can improve your posture; you will look and feel better.</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/lupus.html">
      <content name="title">Lupus</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cutaneous Lupus</content>
      <content name="altTitle">SLE</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Subacute Cutaneous Lupus</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Systemic Lupus Erythematosus</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Discoid lupus</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is lupus?<p>Lupus is a chronic (long-lasting) type of autoimmune disease. Autoimmune diseases happen when your immune <span class="qt1">system</span> attacks healthy cells and tissues by mistake. This attack causes inflammation. It can also damage many parts of the body, including the joints, skin, kidneys, heart, lungs, and brain.</p><p>There are several types of lupus:</p><ul><li>Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is the most common type. It can be mild or severe and can affect many parts of the body.</li><li>Cutaneous lupus affects the skin. It causes a rash or sores, usually after your skin is exposed to sunlight. The two major types of cutaneous lupus are discoid lupus and subacute cutaneous lupus.</li><li>Drug-induced lupus is caused by a reaction to some medicines. The symptoms may start 3 to 6 months after starting the medicine. The symptoms usually go away when you stop taking the medicine.</li><li>Neonatal lupus, which is rare, affects newborns. It is caused by certain antibodies that are passed from the pregnant mother to the fetus.</li></ul>What causes lupus?<p>The cause of lupus is unknown. Researchers are studying what might cause or trigger the disease, such as:</p><ul><li>Genetics</li><li>Environmental factors, such as viral infections, sunlight, certain medicines, and smoking</li><li>Problems with the immune <span class="qt1">system</span></li></ul>Who is more likely to get lupus?<p>Anyone can get lupus, but women get it much more often than men.</p><p>Lupus is more common in African Americans than in White people. It is also more common in people of American Indian and Asian descent.  African American and Hispanic women are more likely to have severe forms of lupus.</p>What are the symptoms of lupus?<p>Lupus can have many symptoms, and they differ from person to person. Some of the more common ones are:</p><ul><li>Arthritis, causing painful and swollen joints and morning stiffness</li><li>Fever</li><li>Fatigue or feeling tired often</li><li>Red rash, most often on the face (also called the "butterfly rash")</li><li>Chest pain when taking a deep breath</li><li>Hair loss</li><li>Pale or purple fingers or toes, from cold and stress (Raynaud phenomenon) </li><li>Sensitivity to the sun</li><li>Swelling in legs or around eyes</li><li>Mouth ulcers</li><li>Swollen glands</li><li>Headache and dizziness</li><li>Confusion and memory problems</li></ul><p>Symptoms may come and go. When you are having symptoms, it is called a flare.  Flares can range from mild to severe. New symptoms may appear at any time.</p>What other problems can lupus cause?<p>Lupus causes inflammation throughout your body. This can cause problems in your organs, including:</p><ul><li>Kidney damage (lupus nephritis).</li><li>Heart problems, including inflammation in the heart (myocarditis), heart valves, or lining of the heart muscle (pericarditis).</li><li>Inflammation of blood vessels (vasculitis).</li><li>Blood clots</li><li>Inflammation of the tissue that surrounds the lungs (pleurisy). This can make it painful to breathe.</li></ul><p>Some people with lupus may be more likely to develop other conditions, such as coronary artery disease (CAD) and atherosclerosis.</p>How is lupus diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test for lupus, and it's often mistaken for other diseases that cause similar symptoms. So it may take a while to get a diagnosis. To find out if you have lupus, your health care provider: </p><ul><li>Will ask about your symptoms, medical history, and family health history</li><li>Will do a complete physical exam</li><li>May order blood tests, such as ANA (antinuclear antibody), antibodies, complete blood count, and complement  tests</li><li>May order other tests, such as urine tests</li><li>May do biopsies:
  <ul><li>Skin biopsy (looking at skin samples under a microscope)</li><li>Kidney biopsy (looking at tissue from your kidney under a microscope)</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the treatments for lupus?<p>There is no cure for lupus, but medicines and lifestyle changes can help control it.</p><p>People with lupus often need to see different providers. You will most likely have a primary care provider and a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in autoimmune and other diseases of the bones, joints, and muscles). Which other specialists you may need depend on how lupus affects your body. For example, if lupus is damaging your heart or blood vessels, you would see a cardiologist (a doctor who specializes in heart diseases).</p><p>Your primary care provider should coordinate care between all of your other providers and treat other problems as they come up. You and your primary care provider will develop a treatment plan to fit your needs. You will both review the plan often to make sure that it is working. You should report new symptoms to your provider right away so that your treatment plan can be changed, if needed.</p><p></p><p>The goals of a treatment plan are to:</p><ul><li>Prevent flares</li><li>Treat flares when they occur</li><li>Reduce organ damage and other problems</li><li>Improve your quality of life</li></ul><p>Treatments may include drugs to:</p><ul><li>Reduce fever, swelling, and pain</li><li>Reduce inflammation in your body</li><li>Prevent or reduce flares</li><li>Reduce or prevent damage to joints</li><li>Suppress (lower) the activity of your immune <span class="qt1">system</span></li></ul><p>Newer medicines are now available for some types of lupus, including lupus that affects the kidneys. These medicines work by targeting specific parts of the immune <span class="qt1">system</span>. Besides taking medicines for lupus, you may need to take medicines for problems that are related to lupus such as high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or infections.</p><p>Alternative and complementary therapies are therapies that are not part of standard treatments. Some people try alternative and complementary therapies to improve their lupus symptoms. But research has not clearly shown whether these treatments may help or treat lupus. Talk to your provider before trying any new treatments.</p><p>Researchers are also studying treatments, such as CAR-T cell therapy, for lupus that hasn't improved with other medicines. New treatments like this are usually only available by joining a research study, until they're approved for general use.</p>How can I cope with lupus?<p>It is important to take an active role in your treatment. It helps to learn more about lupus - being able to spot the warning signs of a flare can help you prevent the flare or make the symptoms less severe.</p><p>It is also important to find ways to cope with the stress of having lupus. Exercising and finding ways to relax may make it easier for you to cope. A good support <span class="qt1">system</span> can also help.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and <span class="qt0">Musculoskeletal</span> and Skin Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/giantcellarteritis.html">
      <content name="title">Giant Cell Arteritis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Temporal Arteritis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Giant cell arteritis is a disorder that causes inflammation of your arteries, usually in the scalp, neck, and arms. It narrows the arteries, which keeps blood from flowing well. Giant cell arteritis often occurs with another disorder called polymyalgia rheumatica. Both are more common in women than in men. They almost always affect people over the age of 50.</p><p>Early symptoms of giant cell arteritis resemble the flu:  fatigue, loss of appetite, and fever. Other symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Headaches</li><li>Pain and tenderness over the temples</li><li>Double vision or visual loss, dizziness</li><li>Problems with coordination and balance</li><li>Pain in your jaw and tongue</li></ul><p>Your doctor will make the diagnosis based on your medical history, symptoms, and a physical exam. There is no specific test for giant cell arteritis, but you may have tests that measure inflammation.</p><p>Treatment is usually with corticosteroids. Early treatment is important; otherwise there is a risk of permanent vision loss or stroke.  However, when properly treated, giant cell arteritis rarely comes back.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and <span class="qt0">Musculoskeletal</span> and Skin Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/rheumatoidarthritis.html">
      <content name="title">Rheumatoid Arthritis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">RA</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is rheumatoid arthritis?<p>Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a form of arthritis that causes pain, swelling, and stiffness in your joints. RA is an autoimmune disease. Although it is most common in the wrist and fingers, this disease can cause your immune <span class="qt1">system</span> to attack any joint tissue. The inflammation (swelling) that comes with RA can also affect other body parts. Inflammation could cause medical issues in your eyes, skin, heart, nerves, blood, or lungs.</p><p>RA differs from osteoarthritis, a common arthritis that often comes with age. RA affects the lining of your joints and damages the tissue that covers the ends of the bones in a joint. Eventually, this might cause your joints to not work as well.</p><p>There is no cure for RA, but early treatment can help you manage symptoms, reduce joint damage, and lead a productive life.</p>Who is more likely to get rheumatoid arthritis?<p>Rheumatoid arthritis can happen at any age, but your risk increases as you become an older adult. Your chance of developing RA can also increase if:</p><ul><li>You're a woman. Women are more likely to get RA than men.</li><li>You have a family history. If a member of your family has RA, you're more likely to get the disease.</li><li>You're a smoker.Smoking over a long period of time increases your risk of getting RA and how serious the disease can be.</li><li>You have other medical conditions that may increase your risk of getting RA. These include obesity, gum disease, and lung disease.</li></ul>What causes rheumatoid arthritis?<p>No one knows what causes rheumatoid arthritis. A few things that might play a part in getting RA include:</p><ul><li>Your genes are parts of DNA in your cells that are passed down from your parents. Certain genes may increase your risk of getting rheumatoid arthritis, but not everyone with these genes gets RA.</li><li>The environment, which includes things such as cigarette smoke, sometimes triggers RA symptoms.</li><li>Hormones are chemical messengers in your bloodstream that control the actions of certain cells or organs. Researchers think that sex hormones might play a role in getting RA. Women are more likely to develop the disease, and RA symptoms may change during and after pregnancy.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis?<p>Your immune <span class="qt1">system</span> may start turning against your body's joints and tissues years before you notice any symptoms of RA. The changes from this type of immune malfunction usually settle in your joints.</p><p>RA affects people differently. You might have the disease for only a short time, or your symptoms might come and go. The severe form can be chronic (long-lasting) and may last a lifetime.</p><p>Symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis may include:</p><ul><li>Joint pain or stiffness when moving. This is usually worse in the morning or after inactivity. RA usually affects both joints. If one of your hands or knees is affected, so is the other.</li><li>Joint tenderness, redness, and warmth.</li><li>Joint swelling may make daily activities hard. These could include things such as combing your hair, buttoning your clothes, or bending your knees.</li><li>Fatigue, fever, and a loss of appetite.</li><li>Hard bumps (rheumatoid nodules) under your skin near the joints.</li></ul>How is rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed?<p>There's no single test for rheumatoid arthritis. The disease develops over time. At first, you may only have a few symptoms, making it hard to diagnose RA in its early stages. To find out if you have RA, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history, including your symptoms.</li><li>Ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had RA.</li><li>Do a physical exam, which includes checking your joints, looking for rashes or nodules, and listening to your chest for signs of inflammation in your lungs.</li><li>Order blood tests or imaging studies (x-ray or ultrasound) to make sure other health conditions aren't causing your symptoms since they may be like other types of arthritis and joint conditions.</li></ul><p>Your provider may refer you to a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in arthritis care) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the treatments for rheumatoid arthritis?<p>There is no cure for RA, but early treatment can help prevent your symptoms from getting worse and damaging your joints. Treatment can include medicine, lifestyle changes, and surgery. These may slow or stop joint damage and reduce pain and swelling.</p><p>Your provider may use a combination of treatments. Your treatment may change based on your symptoms.</p><p>You can help manage your RA symptoms if you:</p><ul><li>Are physically active</li><li>Keep a healthy weight</li><li>Avoid injuries to your joints</li><li>Avoid activities that have repetitive motions, like bending your knee over and over</li><li>Stop smoking, or don't start</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and <span class="qt0">Musculoskeletal</span> and Skin Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ankylosingspondylitis.html">
      <content name="title">Ankylosing Spondylitis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Rheumatoid Spondylitis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Spondylitis, Ankylosing</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is ankylosing spondylitis?<p>Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of arthritis of the spine. It causes inflammation (swelling) between your vertebrae (the bones that make up your spine) and the joints between your spine and pelvis. AS inflammation can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend.</p><p>Symptoms of AS can range from mild to severe back pain. Over time, AS can fuse (grow together) your vertebrae, limiting movement and causing a hunched posture. In some people, AS can affect other joints or body parts.</p><p>There is no cure for AS, but early treatment can help manage symptoms, slow down the disease, and help you lead a more productive life.</p>Who is more likely to get ankylosing spondylitis?<p>Ankylosing spondylitis usually starts before age 45. Early symptoms may begin between the ages of 15 and 30. Your chance of developing AS can also increase if:</p><ul><li>You're a man. AS is more common and severe in men.</li><li>You have a family history. If a member of your family has AS, you're more likely to get the disease.</li><li>You have other medical conditions that may increase your risk of getting AS. These include Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or psoriasis.</li></ul>What causes ankylosing spondylitis?<p>No one knows what causes ankylosing spondylitis, but the environment and genes likely play a role. Your genes are parts of DNA in your cells that are passed down from your parents. Certain genes may increase your risk of getting the disease, but not everyone with these genes gets AS.</p>What are the symptoms of ankylosing spondylitis?<p>AS affects people differently. The most common symptom is pain and stiffness in the lower back and/or hips. The pain is usually worse during the night or after sitting for a long time.</p><p>Over time, AS may progress to other areas of your spine or body. Symptoms may depend on which areas of your body the disease affects. Some people have symptoms that come and go. Others may have severe, ongoing pain.</p><p>Other symptoms of ankylosing spondylitis may include:</p><ul><li>Pain, stiffness, and inflammation of the joints.</li><li>Difficulty taking a deep breath. This could occur if the joints connecting the ribs are affected.</li><li>Changes in vision.</li><li>Fatigue.</li><li>Loss of appetite.</li><li>Weight loss.</li><li>Skin rashes, such as psoriasis.</li><li>Abdominal (belly) pain and loose stools (poop).</li></ul>How is ankylosing spondylitis diagnosed?<p>There is no single test for ankylosing spondylitis. To find out if you have AS your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history, including your symptoms.</li><li>Ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had AS.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or imaging studies.</li></ul>What are the treatments for ankylosing spondylitis?<p>AS has no cure, but treatment may help relieve symptoms, maintain posture, and slow down the disease. Since other parts of your body can be affected by AS, you will likely work with a team of health care professionals for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p><p>Treatment usually includes medicine to help relieve symptoms and keep the disease from getting worse, as well as physical therapy to improve mobility. If AS is severe, surgery may be needed.</p><p>You can help manage your AS symptoms if you:</p><ul><li>Exercise</li><li>Monitor your symptoms</li><li>Manage your stress</li><li>Use assistive devices as needed</li><li>Follow a healthy diet</li><li>Stop smoking, or don't start</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and <span class="qt0">Musculoskeletal</span> and Skin Disease</p></content>
